stem: A real estate agent reports that for homes sold in one neighborhood last year, the mean sale price was $410,000 and the median sale price was $325,000. A buyer asks for the single value that best represents a typical home price. Which response is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Report either one, because the mean and median always give the same typical value.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Report the mean of $410,000, because it accounts for every home's sale price.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Report the median of $325,000, because the mean is pulled above the typical home by a few very expensive sales.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Report the mean of $410,000, because the median ignores half of the data.

rationales.A: Here they differ by $85,000, and a mean well above the median indicates right skew; the two are close mainly when the distribution is roughly symmetric.
rationales.B: Including every value is exactly why the mean is dragged upward by a few very expensive homes; $410,000 is higher than half of the homes sold and so overstates a typical price.
rationales.C: Mean greater than median signals right skew; the median is resistant to the few high-priced homes, so $325,000 better represents a typical sale.
rationales.D: The median is based on the position of the middle value and is not affected by how extreme the other values are; it does not 'ignore' data, it resists outliers.

stem: A student passes the first exam of a course with probability 0.80. If the student passes the first exam, the probability of passing the second exam is 0.75. What is the probability that the student passes both exams?

rationales.A: 0.80 × 0.25 = 0.20 is the probability of passing the first and failing the second.
rationales.B: This treats the problem as finding the chance of passing at least one exam with an addition-rule calculation. The question asks for passing both, which uses the multiplication rule: 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60.
rationales.C: This is only the conditional probability of passing the second exam given the first.

stem: A significance test of H0: p = 0.5 at α = 0.05 has a 0.32 probability of failing to reject H0 when the true proportion is 0.6. What is the power of the test against p = 0.6?

rationales.A: 0.95 = 1 - α is the probability of correctly not rejecting a true H0, not power against p = 0.6.
rationales.B: 0.32 is β, the Type II error probability; power is its complement, 1 - 0.32 = 0.68.
rationales.D: 0.05 is the significance level (the Type I error rate α), not the power. Power is the probability of rejecting H0 when p = 0.6, which is 1 − 0.32 = 0.68.

stem: A school tracks whether students studied and whether they passed. Which expression correctly gives P(studied | passed)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P(studied)P(passed)

choices.label: B
choices.text: P(passed | studied)P(passed)

choices.label: C
choices.text: P(studied) / P(passed | studied)

choices.label: D
choices.text: P(passed | studied)P(studied) / P(passed)

rationales.A: This is P(studied and passed) only if the events are independent, and it is not a conditional probability.
rationales.B: This multiplies by P(passed) rather than dividing by it, so it does not equal P(studied | passed).
rationales.C: The denominator should be the marginal P(passed) and the numerator should be P(passed | studied)P(studied); this inverts the structure.
rationales.D: P(studied and passed)/P(passed), with the numerator rewritten via the multiplication rule.

stem: A researcher has 30 test scores arranged from smallest to largest. Which description locates the median of these scores?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 15th ordered score alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mean of the 15th and 16th ordered scores.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean of the 1st and 30th ordered scores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 16th ordered score alone, since 30/2 + 1 = 16.

rationales.A: Using only the 15th value would be right only if the middle position (n + 1)/2 were exactly 15, which needs n = 29. With 30 values the median averages the 15th and 16th.
rationales.B: With 30 values, the two middle positions are 15 and 16, and the median is their average.
rationales.C: This is the midrange (average of min and max), which is not the median.
rationales.D: The position (n + 1)/2 = 15.5 falls halfway between the 15th and 16th values, so both must be averaged.

stem: Public health data show that in months when ice cream sales are higher, more drownings occur. Which of the following is a plausible confounding variable for this association?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The year in which the data were recorded, with no link to either quantity

choices.label: B
choices.text: The correlation between the monthly ice cream sales and drownings

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hot weather, which draws more people to swim and also increases ice cream purchases

choices.label: D
choices.text: The number of drownings reported in each month

rationales.A: A year with no link to either swimming or ice cream sales does not influence both quantities, so it cannot explain the association and is not a confounder.
rationales.B: The correlation is a summary of the association, not a separate variable acting on both measurements.
rationales.C: A confounder is linked to both variables. Warm weather leads to more swimming (more drownings) and to more ice cream sales, which can produce the association without either causing the other.
rationales.D: This is the response variable itself, not a third variable that influences both quantities.

stem: An insurance company sells a policy for $60. With probability 0.02 it pays a claim of $2,000, and otherwise it pays nothing. What is the company's expected profit per policy, after the claim cost but including the $60 premium?

rationales.A: Expected claim cost = 2,000(0.02) = $40, so expected profit = 60 - 40 = $20.
rationales.B: This is the expected claim cost, 2,000(0.02) = $40, not the expected profit. Profit also includes the $60 premium: 60 − 40 = $20.
rationales.C: The sign is reversed: expected profit is premium minus expected claim cost, 60 - 40 = +20, not 40 - 60.
rationales.D: This is only the premium; the expected payout of $40 per policy was not subtracted.

stem: A set of 8 measurements has a mean of 25. A lab technician replaces one measurement of 10 with a new measurement of 34. How does the mean change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases by 3, because the total rises by 24 and there are 8 measurements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It increases by 24.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases by 2.4, because the 24-point change is spread over 10 measurements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases by 4.5, because the new mean is the average of the old mean, 25, and the new value, 34.

rationales.A: The replacement raises the sum by 34 − 10 = 24, so the mean rises by 24/8 = 3 (from 25 to 28).
rationales.B: 24 is how much the one measurement changed; the mean changes by 24/8 = 3.
rationales.D: Averaging 25 with 34 treats the new value as if it were half of the data. The old mean of 25 summarizes eight values and only one of them changed: the sum rises by 24, so the mean rises by 24/8 = 3.

stem:
A store surveyed 200 customers and recorded age group and whether they bought online. The results are below.
Under 30, bought online: 50
Under 30, did not buy online: 30
30 or older, bought online: 40
30 or older, did not buy online: 80
What is P(under 30 | bought online)?

rationales.A: This divides by the 80 under-30 customers, which is P(bought online | under 30), the reversed conditional.
rationales.B: 90/200 = 0.45 is the marginal probability of buying online. The question asks what fraction of online buyers are under 30, so the numerator must be the 50 under-30 online buyers, not all 90 buyers.
rationales.C: This divides by all 200 customers, giving the joint probability instead of the conditional probability.
rationales.D: Among the 50 + 40 = 90 customers who bought online, 50 are under 30, so P = 50/90 ≈ 0.56.

stem: A random sample of 600 teenagers in a school district is used to build a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all teenagers in the district who own a laptop. The interval is (0.29, 0.35). Which statement is a correct interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 90% of teenagers in the district own a laptop, give or take 3 percentage points.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is a 90% probability that a new random sample of 600 teenagers will have a sample proportion between 0.29 and 0.35.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Between 29% and 35% of the 600 sampled teenagers own a laptop, and we are 90% sure of this.

choices.label: D
choices.text: We are 90% confident that the interval from 0.29 to 0.35 captures the proportion of all teenagers in the district who own a laptop.

rationales.A: The interval estimates the single population proportion; it does not say that 90% of individuals have the characteristic.
rationales.B: The confidence level does not give the probability that a future sample proportion falls in this particular interval; it concerns the method capturing the population proportion.
rationales.C: The sample proportion is known exactly from the data (and lies in the middle of the interval); the interval estimates the population proportion, not the sample's.
rationales.D: The 90% describes how reliably the interval-building method captures the fixed population proportion over many random samples.

stem: A news site reports a 95% confidence interval of (0.53, 0.59) for the proportion of registered voters in a county who favor a school bond, using a random sample of 1,000 voters. Which statement correctly explains what the 95% confidence level means?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 95% of the 1,000 voters in the sample favor the school bond, give or take a few points.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 95% of intervals built this way from repeated random samples would contain the true proportion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is a 5% chance that this sample proportion lies outside the interval from 0.53 to 0.59.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The probability is 0.95 that the true proportion of supporters in the county is exactly 0.56.

rationales.A: The confidence level is not a percentage of individuals; the sample proportion of supporters is near 0.56, not 0.95.
rationales.B: This describes the long-run capture rate of the interval-building method across repeated random samples, which is what the confidence level represents.
rationales.C: The sample proportion is the midpoint of the interval, so it always lies inside it; the 5% refers to intervals that miss the population value.
rationales.D: The true proportion is a single fixed value, and 0.56 is only the sample estimate at the interval's center; the chance of exact equality is not 0.95.

stem: A company surveys a random sample of 1,200 of its customers and computes a 99% confidence interval of (0.72, 0.78) for the proportion of all its customers who are satisfied. Which statement is a correct interpretation of this interval?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 99% of the 1,200 surveyed customers gave a satisfaction rating between 0.72 and 0.78.

choices.label: B
choices.text: We are 99% confident that the true proportion of all the company's customers who are satisfied is between 0.72 and 0.78.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is a 99% probability that the next customer surveyed will be satisfied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The true proportion of satisfied customers changes from sample to sample and falls between 0.72 and 0.78 in 99% of samples.

rationales.A: The interval gives plausible values for a population proportion; it does not describe how individual customers' ratings are distributed.
rationales.B: The 99% refers to the reliability of the method: about 99% of intervals constructed this way capture the true customer-satisfaction proportion.
rationales.C: The interval says nothing about 0.99 as a probability for one customer; the estimated proportion satisfied is about 0.75.
rationales.D: The population proportion is fixed; it is the interval that changes from sample to sample.

stem: A cafe records 300 orders. Of these, 120 included coffee, 90 included a pastry, and 45 included both. For a randomly chosen order, are 'includes coffee' and 'includes a pastry' independent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because 45 does not equal 120 + 90 = 210.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, because 120 + 90 = 210, which is less than the 300 orders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because the 45 orders with both are fewer than the 120 or the 90 orders with each item.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because P(coffee and pastry) = 45/300 = 0.15, which differs from P(coffee)P(pastry) = 0.40 x 0.30 = 0.12.

rationales.A: Independence is not tested by comparing the joint count to the sum of counts; the joint probability is compared with the product.
rationales.B: Whether the counts sum to less than the total says nothing about how the events relate.
rationales.C: A joint count is smaller than each single count for almost any two events, so this says nothing about independence; independence compares the joint probability with the product of the individual probabilities.
rationales.D: Independence needs the joint probability to equal the product of the individual probabilities; 0.15 is not 0.12.

stem: A factory knows that 12% of its widgets are defective. An inspector randomly selects n = 400 widgets. What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion of defective widgets?

rationales.B: The square root applies to the whole fraction p(1-p)/n, not just to n; the correct value is about 0.016.
rationales.C: This drops (1 - p); sqrt(0.12/400) is about 0.017, which is not the correct standard error.
rationales.D: This is the variance 0.000264; the square root was never taken.
